summary.text: Lesson 4 of Wordly Wise 3000 Book 9: fifteen words covering manner and character (punctilious, wry, Spartan, sedentary), motion and disorder (meander, hubbub, contend), and everyday nouns (adage, camaraderie, paraphernalia), plus extraneous, odoriferous, recuperate, regale and temporal.

why.text: Several of these — wry, Spartan, odoriferous — are words writers reach for when they want to imply something without stating it. They are as much about tone as about meaning.

objectives.text: Define and use all fifteen Lesson 4 words correctly
Pick the correct sense of a two-sense word from what follows the verb
Identify synonym, antonym and “lacks” relationships in analogies
Notice when a formally neutral word is carrying an implied judgement

parentNote.text: Built from the Lesson 4 word list. Contend is the one worth checking she has straight: it means both “struggle with” and “assert”, and the way to tell is what follows the verb. The analogies reuse the “lacks” relationship from Lesson 3 on purpose — naming the same relationship in a new place is what makes the skill transfer rather than stay a trick.

nextUp.text: Cards, then the quiz. Tap 🔊 on camaraderie and paraphernalia — both are easier to say than to read.

cards.def:
**An old saying that has come to be accepted as true; a proverb.** (noun)
• Preparing to move again, we comforted ourselves with the adage "A rolling stone gathers no moss."
• Its age is part of the definition — a clever line you invent today is not an adage.

**Good will and warm feelings among friends.** (noun)
• A spirit of camaraderie filled the room at the high-school reunion.
• It describes the feeling in a GROUP, not between two people.

**To struggle with.** (verb)
• Mail carriers sometimes have to contend with bothersome dogs.
• Second meaning: to maintain or assert — opponents contend the risk is too great.
cards.hint: Two senses that feel unrelated but are not: both involve pushing against something.

cards.def:
**Not necessary; irrelevant.** (adjective)
• When you revise your instructions, eliminate any extraneous details.
• Extra hides inside it — extraneous material is surplus to the point.

**Noisy confusion; uproar.** (noun)
• Fans thronged onto the field in a hubbub of excitement when their team won the pennant.
• Both halves matter: it is noise AND disorder together.

**To follow a winding course.** (verb)
• The Mississippi meanders from northern Minnesota to the Gulf of Mexico.
• Second meaning: to wander aimlessly — shoppers meandered through the sidewalk sale.

**Having or giving off a smell.** (adjective)
• Odoriferous fumes spewed from the truck's exhaust.
• Strictly it is neutral, though it usually turns up describing bad smells.

**Personal belongings; equipment associated with a particular activity.** (noun)
• We accumulated so much paraphernalia that the closets could not hold it all.
• We keep our riding paraphernalia in the barn.

**Careful of and attentive to details, especially ones relating to good manners.** (adjective)
• A punctilious host tries to leave nothing to chance when preparing for guests.
• Related to punctual — both come from a root meaning point.
cards.hint: Punctilious people care about the small points, especially social ones.

cards.def:
**To regain health or strength.** (verb)
• Her doctor expects Amanda to recuperate quickly.
• It names the PROCESS of getting better, not the moment of being well.

**To entertain or delight.** (verb)
• Dishi regaled his friends with his funny stories.
• Usually followed by *with* — you regale someone WITH something.

**Doing or requiring a lot of sitting.** (adjective)
• Operating a computer is sedentary work.
• It describes the activity or the person, never the furniture.

**Marked by simplicity and lack of luxury.** (adjective)
• The sergeant described the Spartan way of life to the new recruits.
• From ancient Sparta, whose citizens were famous for austerity — which is why it keeps its capital letter.

**Relating to the everyday world as opposed to the spiritual or eternal.** (adjective)
• Medieval kings were the temporal rulers of their states but accepted the Pope's authority in religious matters.
• Worldly, in other words — the affairs of this life.

**Turned or bent to one side in distaste or humour; amusing in a quiet, sharp way.** (adjective)
• He gave a wry smile as he admitted believing such a far-fetched tale.
• Wry humour is dry and slightly twisted — it never announces itself.

opts: An old saying accepted as true
A piece of equipment for an activity
A period of rest after illness
questions.hint: Think of a proverb your grandparents might quote.
steps: An adage is an old saying that has come to be accepted as true.
"A rolling stone gathers no moss" is the book's own example.
The wrong options define hubbub, paraphernalia and recuperation.

ex.main: **An old saying accepted as true.** Age is part of the definition — a new clever line is not yet an adage.
ex.tip: Adage, maxim and proverb overlap heavily. If a question offers more than one, look for what makes them differ.

opts: Details that are unnecessary to the point
Details that are difficult to understand
questions.hint: Extra is hiding inside the word.
steps: Extraneous means not necessary; irrelevant.
Revising instructions by eliminating extraneous details means cutting what does not serve the point.
Extraneous information can be perfectly true and perfectly clear — it is simply beside the point.

ex.main: **Unnecessary to the point.** Note that extraneous does NOT mean false — that is the trap.
ex.tip: Watch for options that sound similar but change the claim. Irrelevant and untrue are very different accusations.

questions.hint: Think of what "sedan" and "sediment" have in common.
steps: Sedentary means doing or requiring a lot of sitting.
Operating a computer is the book's example of sedentary work.
Travel, location and pay are unrelated to the word.

ex.main: **Work involving a lot of sitting.** The root is the Latin for sit — the same root under sediment, which settles.
ex.tip: Latin roots repay learning once: sed- (sit) shows up in sedentary, sediment, sedan and session.

questions.hint: It is about a body, not an object.
steps: Recuperate means to regain health or strength.
A doctor expecting Amanda to recuperate quickly is talking about her recovery.
Recovering a lost object is a different word entirely, despite sounding close.

ex.main: **Regain health or strength.** Recuperate names the process of getting better, not the finished state.
ex.tip: Recuperate and recover overlap, but recuperate is specifically about health. The nearby option is the trap.

opts: Warm good will among a group of friends
questions.hint: Comrade is sitting inside the word.
steps: Camaraderie is good will and warm feelings among friends.
A reunion filled with a spirit of camaraderie is a room full of that feeling.
It is the opposite of rivalry and unrelated to formal agreements.

ex.main: **Warm good will among friends.** It describes the atmosphere of a GROUP rather than a single friendship.
ex.tip: Comrade hides inside camaraderie and gives you both the meaning and the spelling.

opts: Filled with the smell of cooking
questions.hint: Named after a famously tough ancient city.
steps: Spartan means marked by simplicity and lack of luxury.
The word comes from ancient Sparta, whose citizens were known for austerity.
A Spartan room is bare by choice, which is why the word keeps its capital letter.

ex.main: **Simple and without luxury.** Sparta earned the adjective by living that way on purpose.
ex.tip: Words made from place names keep their capitals: Spartan, Herculean, Draconian. That is a spelling rule you can rely on.

questions.q: A coach tells the team "you will have to contend with rain and a heavy field." She means the team will have to:
opts: Argue that the conditions are unfair
Report the conditions to the referee
questions.hint: Contend has two senses. Which fits this sentence?
steps: Contend can mean to struggle with, or to maintain and assert.
Here the object is rain and a heavy field — conditions, not claims.
You cannot assert a rainy field; you can only struggle against it.
So the "struggle with" sense is the one the sentence needs.

ex.main: **Struggle against those conditions.** The object of the verb tells you which sense is live.
ex.tip: For two-sense words, look at what follows the verb. Contend WITH conditions is struggle; contend THAT something is true is assert.

opts: He was punctilious about thank-you notes, writing each one the same evening
She was punctilious and arrived nearly an hour late
The punctilious storm knocked out power across the county
He gave a punctilious shrug and walked away
questions.hint: It is about attention to small points, especially social ones.
steps: Punctilious means careful of and attentive to details, especially details of good manners.
Writing every thank-you note the same evening is exactly that kind of care.
Arriving late contradicts the word, and storms and shrugs cannot be attentive to manners.

ex.main: **Writing every thank-you note promptly.** Punctilious is about social precision, not just general tidiness.
ex.tip: Punctilious and punctual are cousins but not twins: one is about manners, the other only about time.

questions.q: A memoirist writes that her uncle "regaled the table with stories until the candles burned down." This tells you the uncle:
steps: Regale means to entertain or delight.
Regaling the table means his stories were enjoyed, not endured.
"Until the candles burned down" confirms it: people stayed.

ex.main: **Entertained everyone at length.** Regale carries approval — a boring speaker cannot regale anyone.
ex.tip: The detail after a verb often confirms its tone. Candles burning down means nobody left, which rules out boredom.

questions.hint: What does a Spartan room not have?
steps: Spartan means marked by a LACK of luxury — the adjective names what is absent.
So the pattern is: adjective : the thing it lacks.
Extraneous means lacking necessity — it is material that is not needed. Match.
An adage is a kind of saying, regale and entertain are synonyms, and recuperating follows an illness rather than lacking one.

ex.main: **Both pairs are ADJECTIVE : WHAT IT LACKS.** Spartan surroundings have no luxury; extraneous details have no necessity.
ex.tip: This is the same "lacks" relationship as WANTON : RESTRAINT. Once you can name a relationship, it starts appearing everywhere.

questions.hint: How close in meaning are these two?
steps: To meander is to wander — following a winding course or drifting aimlessly.
So the relationship is: near-synonyms.
To contend (in one of its senses) is to struggle. Same meaning. Match.
Sedentary and active are opposites; punctilious people attend to detail; camaraderie exists among friends.

ex.main: **Both pairs are SYNONYMS.** Meander and wander overlap almost completely; so do contend and struggle.
ex.tip: When a stem word has two senses, the analogy usually rides on one of them. Meander here is the aimless sense.

questions.hint: These two describe opposite attitudes to detail.
steps: Punctilious means highly attentive to detail; careless means the reverse.
So the stem pair is opposites.
Sedentary (sitting) and active (moving) are likewise opposites. Match.
Meander and wander are synonyms, an adage contains wisdom, and wry describes a kind of humour.

ex.main: **Both pairs are ANTONYMS.** Punctilious versus careless and sedentary versus active are both straight reversals.
ex.tip: Check every option for an opposite before settling. Here only one pair actually reverses; the others just feel related.

questions.q: A travel writer describes a village as "odoriferous, in the way of places where fish is the whole economy." What is the writer doing with that word?
opts: Naming a strong smell without flatly calling it unpleasant
Praising the village for its cleanliness
Complaining that the village has no industry
Saying the village has no particular character
questions.hint: Odoriferous is technically neutral. Why choose it here?
steps: Odoriferous strictly means having or giving off a smell — neutral in the dictionary.
But it usually turns up describing bad smells, so readers hear the implication.
The clause about fish supplies the reason without the writer ever saying "it stinks".
That is the move: the neutral word carries the judgement, and the writer keeps clean hands.

ex.main: **Naming a smell while declining to insult the village outright.** The neutral word does the work an insulting word would have done.
ex.tip: Writers pick formally neutral words to imply things deniably. Noticing that gap is a real reading skill.

questions.q: Which Lesson 4 word would BEST replace the underlined phrase: "She accepted the criticism with a *quietly amused, slightly twisted* smile"?
questions.hint: One of these words means exactly that kind of smile.
steps: The phrase describes amusement that is quiet and a little bent to one side.
Wry means precisely that: turned to one side in humour, amusing in a quiet, sharp way.
The other three describe attention to manners, sitting, and smell — none of them describes a smile.

ex.main: **Wry.** The whole phrase collapses into one word, which is what good vocabulary buys you.
ex.tip: When a test hands you a long descriptive phrase, one vocabulary word usually replaces it exactly. Find that word.

opts: A short saying accepted as true
questions.hint: Two things at once: noise and disorder.
steps: A hubbub is noisy confusion; uproar.
Fans thronging the field in a hubbub of excitement is noise and disorder together.
Quiet order is its opposite; the other options define meander and adage.

ex.main: **Noisy confusion or uproar.** Both halves are required — orderly noise is not a hubbub.
ex.tip: Some definitions bundle two conditions. Check that an example satisfies both before accepting it.

questions.q: Temporal authority refers to power over:
questions.hint: It is set against the spiritual.
steps: Temporal means relating to the everyday world as opposed to the spiritual or eternal.
Medieval kings held temporal power while the Pope held religious authority.
The word exists precisely to draw that line, so the religious option is the reverse of the answer.

ex.main: **Everyday, worldly matters.** Temporal is defined by what it is NOT — the spiritual or eternal.
ex.tip: Words defined by contrast are best learned with their opposite attached: temporal versus spiritual, always as a pair.

questions.q: A shop sells "cycling paraphernalia." This means it sells:
opts: The gear and equipment associated with cycling
Books about the history of cycling
questions.hint: Paraphernalia is the stuff that goes WITH an activity.
steps: Paraphernalia means personal belongings, or equipment associated with a particular activity.
Riding paraphernalia kept in a barn is the book's own example.
So cycling paraphernalia is the surrounding gear — helmets, pumps, lights — not the bicycles alone.

ex.main: **The gear and equipment that go with cycling.** Paraphernalia names the accompanying kit rather than the main object.
ex.tip: Paraphernalia is always plural in feel and slightly sprawling in meaning — it suggests a lot of assorted stuff.

questions.q: A reviewer writes that a novel "meanders for two hundred pages before finding its subject." The reviewer means the novel:
opts: Wanders without clear direction for a long stretch
Repeats the same scene several times
Is written in an old-fashioned style
questions.hint: Which sense of meander fits a book rather than a river?
steps: Meander means to follow a winding course, or to wander aimlessly.
Applied to a narrative, the aimless sense is the live one.
"Before finding its subject" confirms the criticism: for two hundred pages it had none.
That is wandering without direction, not speed, repetition or style.

ex.main: **Wanders without clear direction.** A meandering river is neutral; a meandering novel is a complaint.
ex.tip: The same word can be neutral about landscape and critical about writing. Ask what is being described before deciding tone.
